extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, critics, and practicing artists interested in principles of landscape painting
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and evaluative standards for producing and judging landscape painting, emphasizing truthful representation of natural particulars, compositional unity, and the moral/aesthetic aims of art. Focuses on botanical, geological, and meteorological knowledge, detail-handling, idealization, and unity of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of the artist / self-annihilation
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist has done nothing till he has concealed himself; the power of the masters is shown by their self-annihilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work should so wholly direct attention to its subject that the spectator thinks not of the artist or his methods; the mark of greatness is when the maker is invisible in the work. Examples invoked: great poets/dramatists (Aeschylus, Shakespeare) whose skill is not the focus of the audience's thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should exalt nature (not showcase technical dexterity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiration should be for the perfection of nature, not for the artist's skill or 'trickeries'; paintings should tend toward the honor of God/nature rather than the honor of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid producing works that merely exhibit the dexterities of individuals or systems. If spectators leave praising the artist’s method rather than feeling reverence for nature, the work belongs to a mistaken school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect knowledge and simple, unencumbered rendering of specific characters
rubrics_metrics.description: There is but one grand style...based on the perfect knowledge, and consists in the simple, unencumbered rendering, of the specific characters of the given object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grandeur depends on faithfully rendering the species-character of each object (man, beast, flower, rock, cloud) simply and directly rather than inventing or obscuring those characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject caricature and abandonment of specific form
rubrics_metrics.description: Every change, caricature, or abandonment of such specific character, is as destructive of grandeur as it is of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid alterations of natural features arising from 'powerless indolence or blind audacity' — such violations produce monstrosity, disorganization, and loss of beauty and propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: The true ideal of landscape is the specific (type) perfected, not impossible invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The true ideal of landscape ... is the expression of the specific--not the individual, but the specific--characters of every object, in their perfection; there is an ideal form of every herb, flower, and tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idealization should mean seizing the type (the perfected generic form) and rendering it purely and simply; e.g., Titian simplifies hues and omits accidental marks while keeping type-specific characters. Do not invent impossible combinations to produce an 'ideal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and render botanical detail appropriately for expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Every landscape painter should know the specific characters of every object he has to represent, rock, flower, or cloud; and in his highest ideal works, all their distinctions will be perfectly expressed ... according to the nature of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foregrounds and salient parts demand botanical fidelity when they contribute to expression; examples: Titian and Raphael render stamens and leaves with exquisite accuracy when those details serve the picture's meaning. Details should be rendered with degree suited to their role (severe simplicity for sublime, refined finish for beauty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific (geologic & meteorologic) accuracy of inorganic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Every class of rock, earth and cloud, must be known by the painter, with geologic and meteorologic accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different geological formations and climates produce distinct landscape orders (marsh, chalk, limestone, primary mountains) with incommunicable characters; accurate knowledge of these distinctions produces truthful, harmonious landscape character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Details must serve a greater unity; not sought for their own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not, therefore, detail sought for its own sake ... which constitute great art ... but it is detail referred to a great end -- sought for the sake of the inestimable beauty which exists in the slightest things, and treated in a manly, broad, and impressive manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid Denner-like minute portraiture of matter (counting crystals, isolated texture) unless such minutiae contribute to the picture's unified expressive purpose. Details that are perfect but unreferred to final purpose indicate tyro's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile detail and whole; aim for both specificity and breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The rapid and powerful artist ... looks with contempt on those who seek minutiae ... yet the last step in art reconciles details and the whole so both become compatible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists must learn to balance breadth and finely observed particulars; the consummate master makes details contribute to the life and beauty of the entire composition rather than destroying unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ignorant generalization; generalize only from knowledge of distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: That generalization then is right, true, and noble, which is based on the knowledge of the distinctions and observance of the relations of individual kinds. That generalization is wrong, false, and contemptible, which is based on ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not collapse distinct kinds (rocks, trees, climates) into a bland 'general' type through ignorance or laziness; true generalization comes from understanding specific differences and relating them coherently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of feeling and propriety of relations in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The power and grandeur of [a picture] will be exactly proportioned to the unity of feeling manifested in its several parts, and to the propriety and simplicity of the relations in which they stand to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every element unnecessary to the picture is an encumbrance; contradictory facts and unharmonious accumulations destroy impressiveness. Apply principles of historical composition: unity, economy, and sympathy among parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose differing landscape orders only with severe judgment and natural links
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter ... has the choice of either working out the isolated character of some one distinct class of scene, or of bringing together a multitude of different elements, which may adorn each other by contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining different landscape types, ensure they are connected by natural links and governed by strict judgment; contrast can enhance but must be a point, not equalized opposition. Failure yields the motley, implausible 'ideal' landscape (anti-pattern: Claude's Il Mulino example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealization: simplify hues and omit accidental particulars while preserving type
rubrics_metrics.description: The master does not aim at the particular color of individual blossoms; he seizes the type of all, and gives it with the utmost purity and simplicity of which color is capable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idealization is achieved by selecting and purifying the characteristics that define the species (type), omitting accidental details like dew-drops or insects that do not contribute to the ideal expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use knowledge as means to expression, not as an end in itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Every kind of knowledge may be sought from ignoble motives ... The one notes their distinctions for the sake of swelling his herbarium, the other, that he may render them vehicles of expression and emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific and detailed study (botany, geology, meteorology) is valuable only insofar as it enables the painter to render expressive, emotive, and truthful pictures; avoid accumulating facts for curiosity alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreground particulars should not be omitted because they are less obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinctive forms of vegetable life are indeed less obvious and less obtrusive; for which very reason there is less excuse for omitting them, because there is less danger of their disturbing the attention or engaging the fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not excuse omission of subtle botanical or textural detail by claiming the viewer won't notice; those particulars often enrich understanding and expression without distracting from the primary subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assembling incompatible particulars to construct an 'ideal' landscape
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'ideal' landscape ... a group of the artist's studies from nature, individually spoiled, selected with such opposition of character as may insure their neutralizing each other's effect, and united with sufficient unnaturalness and violence of association to insure their producing a general sensation of the impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: cobbling together disparate studies (mismatched geology, architecture, figures, and atmosphere) produces scenes that are impossible and incoherent (example analysis of Claude's Il Mulino); the ideal must be consistent with natural relations.
